<reason>PRO built a clean population-level causal story (everyone got heavier at once, so the current not the swimmers) and then defended it with two moves CON never squarely neutralized: (1) the scale/dose-response critique — CON's best evidence is supervised, intensive programs whose effects evaporate when stripped down to reach a nation, and CON's own late retreat to "supervised programs" in B4.1 walked into it; and (2) the asymmetry of compensation — a reformulated supply benefits people passively while coaching effects decay by default. PRO also turned CON's own "turning point" standard against forty years of behavioural guidance, and CON's answer (B4.1) was to drop the standard rather than meet it, effectively conceding the pressure question. CON's strongest material — the whack-a-mole/infinite-regress and "capacity that travels" framing — was genuinely thoughtful, but PRO's reply that "snacking elsewhere" means the shelf decides what substitution is made of was a sharp, damaging reframe CON only reasserted against rather than answered. CON's "shelf changed, body didn't" was an assertion without support, and its opening was clipped. Both sides used plausible background knowledge without fake precision, but PRO made the debate easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A4.1–A4.5 (answering the pressure questions): PRO accepted apps onto CON's ledger, applied CON's own "bend the curve" test to them, then distinguished the two compensations as running in opposite directions (passive benefit vs. default decay) and turned CON's "snacking elsewhere" into a concession that the environment determines substitution. CON's B4.1 response — abandoning the turning-point standard because it disqualifies both sides — confirmed rather than repaired the damage.</best_rebuttal>
